A mutex (the name comes from "mutual exclusion") is a synchronization primitive that protects a critical section, meaning a piece of code that works with shared data and can't safely be run by more than one thread at a time. Before a thread enters the critical section, it acquires (locks) the mutex, and when it leaves, it releases it. Only one thread can hold a mutex at any moment. If another thread tries to acquire it in the meantime, that thread waits until the mutex is released. This keeps updates to shared state from interleaving and corrupting each other.

Mutexes are also easy to get wrong. Say thread A holds one lock and is waiting for a second, while thread B holds the second and is waiting for the first. Neither can move forward, and the program hangs. This is called a deadlock. The standard ways to avoid it are to acquire locks in the same order everywhere and to keep them held for as short a time as you can.

Speed is a concern as well, because concurrent code locks and unlocks all the time. Linux builds its mutexes on the futex, short for "fast userspace mutex." If no other thread is competing for the lock, a futex can acquire and release it using only atomic operations in user space. It makes a system call into the kernel only when a thread actually needs to be put to sleep or woken up.
